Rocket.Chat Livechat file-upload ID enumeration sweep (ObjectId harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts an unauthenticated source pulling many distinct /file-upload/{fileId} objects while carrying the Livechat authorization params (rc_room_type=l + rc_token) — the continuous ObjectId-prediction harvest described in the Aikido disclosure. High volume of distinct fileIds from one IP via the Livechat auth path is the signature of the mass file-capture exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit request shape from the article's Python PoC — GET /file-upload/{fileId} with rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — combined with a distinct-fileId volume threshold that captures the 'retrieve all generated valid IDs continuously' harvest. Legit Livechat file access does not fan out across dozens of unrelated fileIds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/rocketchat-security-fixes-updates-and-advisories • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely busy Livechat helpdesk session where a visitor downloads many attachments the agent sent (all belonging to that room)
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor health-checking a file-upload URL repeatedly (usually one fixed path, not distinct fileIds)
  • Internal backup or migration tooling iterating over uploads with a service token
  • Authorized DAST/vulnerability scanner (Aikido, Burp) replaying the PoC against a staging instance
  • CDN origin prefetch pulling attachments
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","UptimeRobot","Pingdom")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the requests carry rc_room_type=l + rc_token and hit many DISTINCT fileIds, and check whether the Rocket.Chat build predates 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and if patch is not yet deployed, disable Livechat (Admin > Omnichannel) or upgrade immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate which fileIds returned HTTP 200 to that IP to scope leaked files, and search for the same IP creating anonymous visitors (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor) to identify the session token used.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and (Url has "rc_room_type=l" or Url has "rc_token=")
| extend FileId = extract(@"/file-upload/([^/?]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(FileId)
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(FileId), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctFiles >= 25   // >=25 distinct file-upload IDs fetched via the Livechat auth path from one source in 1h = ObjectId harvest sweep
| order by DistinctFiles desc

Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.

| where VisitorReg >= 1 and RoomReq >= 1 and FileReq >= 1   // same source bootstraps an anon visitor+room then reads uploads within 10m
| order by FileReq desc

Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) AIExploitation Medium
Single-event signature for the Rocket.Chat access-control bypass: a GET to /file-upload/ whose query string carries rc_room_type=l together with rc_token — the Livechat authorization path being used to read a file, exactly as in the disclosed exploit. Surfaces individual exploit attempts even below the harvest threshold. Rationale: Uses the verbatim exploit primitive from the PoC — /file-upload/ path plus rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — as an atomic, Sigma-portable signature. It matches even a single probe, complementing the volume- and chain-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Livechat visitor downloading an attachment shared in their own helpdesk room (identical request shape)
  • Rocket.Chat client appending rc_room_type/rc_token to file URLs during normal Livechat file rendering
  • WAF or SSL-inspection proxy replaying the request as part of active response testing
  • Authorized researcher/DAST scan on a staging instance
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl bot following a Livechat file link
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — HTTP 200 means a file was served; note the SrcIpAddr, Content-Disposition filename, and whether the source ever authenticated. 2) Contain: if the instance is unpatched (pre 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13), upgrade or disable Livechat and block the IP. 3) Hunt: aggregate this IP's requests to see if it escalates into the distinct-fileId harvest sweep, and correlate with anonymous visitor registrations from the same address.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and Url has "rc_room_type=l" and Url has "rc_token="
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Twig SSTI markers in request-controlled fields against Craft/Formie public forms AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests carrying Twig template syntax ({{ }}, {% %}) in the User-Agent, Referer, or query string reaching a Craft CMS site running Formie. CVE-2026-52889 copies these request-derived Hidden-field defaults straight into Craft's Twig render layer, so Twig markers in these fields are the earliest observable of exploitation of a public form. Rationale: Uses the exact request-derived input surface named in the advisory (User Agent, Referer, Current URL, Query Parameter) and Twig delimiters {{ / {% (plus URL-encoded %7b%7b). Web-request telemetry only exists in Sentinel W3CIISLog / Splunk Web DM; Defender AH, Datadog standard sources, Falcon FDR and CloudWatch do not carry HTTP request headers, so those queries are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against the sibling Formie SSTI advisory CVE-2026-45697 and the Craft SSTI advisory GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-formie-plugin-twig-injection-via-hidden-field-cve-2026-45697-critical/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) sending {{7*7}} SSTI probes
  • Client-side JS frameworks (AngularJS/Vue/Mustache) passing {{ }} template strings in query params
  • Marketing/analytics referrers containing mustache placeholders like {{campaign}}
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the public form
  • URLs carrying JSON blobs with doubled braces
Suppression filter
| where scStatus == 200 and csUriStem !contains "/api/" and csUserAgent !has_any ("AngularJS","Vue")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the window; confirm the target csUriStem is a page that renders a Formie form and whether scStatus==200 (server processed the payload vs 404/403). Decode the payload from UA/query/cookie. 2) Contain: if the payload contains RCE gadgets or scStatus 200 on a form page, block the source IP at the WAF and confirm Formie is on 3.1.27+; if not, apply the workaround (remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults) immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php/w3wp spawning shells (UC3) and review the same source IP for gadget strings (UC2).

     or csReferer contains "{{" or csReferer contains "{%"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Active Twig RCE gadget strings in Craft/Formie HTTP request inputs AIExploitation High
High-fidelity detection for Twig-to-PHP RCE gadgets (_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback / getFilter / craft.app) delivered via the request-controlled Hidden-field defaults exploited by CVE-2026-52889. Unlike generic {{ }} probing, these tokens are unambiguous command-execution attempts. Rationale: Anchors on the documented Twig RCE gadget chain _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback + getFilter and Craft's exposed craft.app object — these strings virtually never appear in benign traffic, so this warrants alerting. Web-request headers/query are only available in Sentinel/Splunk web logs; Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch do not carry them. Gadget syntax corroborated via PayloadsAllTheThings PHP SSTI and the Craft SSTI advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://swisskyrepo.github.io/PayloadsAllTheThings/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/PHP/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw

Craft/PHP/IIS web worker spawning a command shell (Formie SSTI RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the PHP FastCGI, php-fpm, or IIS worker process backing a Craft CMS site spawning a command interpreter or recon LOLBin — the post-exploitation footprint of a successful Twig SSTI RCE via CVE-2026-52889. A web worker launching cmd/powershell/sh is not normal Craft behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the specific web-tier parents of a Craft/PHP deployment (php-cgi.exe, php-fpm, w3wp.exe backing IIS+FastCGI, nginx/httpd) spawning shells/recon LOLBins — the concrete execution outcome of the Twig system()/exec gadget the advisory warns can lead to RCE. Purely endpoint telemetry, so no web-log or CloudWatch query. Not covered by generic Office-spawn-script or encoded-PS rules. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running Craft console commands (php craft resave/queue/run) that legitimately shell out
  • Image-processing plugins (ImageMagick/GD) invoked by php calling system utilities
  • Deployment/build steps (composer, npm) executed under the web-service account
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched by the web worker
  • Scheduled Craft queue jobs spawning curl for outbound webhooks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "craft" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("queue/run","resave","gc","migrate")) and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a shell running whoami/id/net/certutil under the web-service account with no interactive admin session is high-signal; correlate the timestamp with UC1/UC2 web-log hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the child process, and revoke/rotate any credentials accessible to the web-service account; confirm Formie is patched to 3.1.27+. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the php/w3wp worker (webshells), outbound connections from the worker process, new local accounts or scheduled tasks, and repeat the process-tree hunt across all other Craft/Formie web nodes.

Threat Actors Probe Gitea Docker Flaw CVE-2026-20896 13 Days After Disclosure

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a recently patched critical security flaw in Gitea Docker images, according to Sysdig. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-20896 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that stems from the DevOps platform trusting the "X-WEBAUTH-USER" header from any source IP address, effectively allowing an unauthenticated internet client to get elevated

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Gitea CVE-2026-20896 probe source IP 159.26.98.241 (ProtonVPN) contact · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gitea CVE-2026-20896 auth bypass: X-WEBAUTH-USER header from untrusted source · [LLM] Vulnerable Gitea (≤1.26.2) exposed to CVE-2026-20896
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gitea CVE-2026-20896 auth bypass: X-WEBAUTH-USER header from untrusted source AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Gitea instance carrying the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any non-loopback / non-trusted-proxy source IP. This is the exact single-header exploit for CVE-2026-20896, where the Docker image's REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=* default lets any client impersonate any user (admin, gitea_admin) with no password or token. Rationale: Anchors on the literal exploit primitive named in the article and GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4: the X-WEBAUTH-USER header. Defender/Falcon left empty because EDR endpoint telemetry does not capture HTTP request headers; this detection lives in web/proxy/WAF logs. The loopback-exclusion in Sentinel keeps the legitimate trusted-proxy path (127.0.0.0/8) quiet. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/gitea-forgejo-nine-cves-1263-security-release-2026/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse-proxy auth (Authelia, oauth2-proxy, Cloudflare Access) genuinely injecting X-WEBAUTH-USER from the trusted loopback/proxy IP
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, internal pentest) sending the header as an exploit check
  • Load balancer or uptime health checks replaying a stored request template that includes the header
  • Internal admin testing/validating the reverse-proxy authentication configuration after patching
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full request — note the SourceIP, the X-WEBAUTH-USER value (admin/gitea_admin = high risk), and whether the request bypassed the proxy (direct hit on the container port). Confirm the Gitea build is ≤1.26.2. Step 2 (contain): If the source is external/untrusted, block the IP at the WAF/firewall, force-expire active Gitea sessions, and either set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 or upgrade to 1.26.3+. Step 3 (hunt): Review Gitea audit logs for admin actions (new SSH keys, tokens, webhooks, repo clones) tied to that session; enumerate all repos accessed since first probe; rotate any secrets/tokens the impersonated account could read.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestContext has "X-WEBAUTH-USER" or Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea CVE-2026-20896 probe source IP 159.26.98.241 (ProtonVPN) contact AIReconnaissance Medium
Alerts on any network connection to/from 159.26.98.241, the ProtonVPN egress IP Sysdig observed making the first in-the-wild probe against internet-facing Gitea instances for CVE-2026-20896. Scoped to Gitea/web-facing hosts. Rationale: Uses the single network IOC the article provides (159.26.98.241). Confidence held at Medium because it is a shared ProtonVPN egress cited only by Sysdig/THN and may be reused by benign users or rotate — hence the host-scoping and analyst-verify runbook rather than auto-block. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threat-actors-probe-gitea-docker-flaw.html • https://dailysecurityreview.com/resources/gitea-cve-2026-20896-auth-bypass-exploited-via-one-http-header/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote developer or admin browsing to Gitea over ProtonVPN sharing the same egress IP
  • Security researchers or benign internet-wide scanners (Shodan, Censys) transiting the same VPN pool
  • VPN egress reassignment over time making the IOC stale and matching unrelated traffic
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox infrastructure that replays IOCs for validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the local asset is an internet-facing Gitea/web host and check the connection direction and port — inbound to the Gitea HTTP port is the concern. Correlate with UC1 (X-WEBAUTH-USER header) for the same timeframe. Step 2 (contain): If tied to a header-bypass request or admin action, block 159.26.98.241 at the perimeter and expire Gitea sessions; if it is only a benign browse from a known dev, allowlist the user, not the IP. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 30 days of firewall/WAF logs for the same IP against all web assets, and check whether the same source attempted other Gitea endpoints (/admin, /api/v1/admin).

Vulnerable Gitea (≤1.26.2) exposed to CVE-2026-20896 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt surfacing hosts running Gitea versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-20896 (fixed in 1.26.3) via vulnerability-management telemetry, so they can be patched or reconfigured before the header bypass is weaponized against them. Rationale: Pins the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-20896) and patched build (1.26.3) from the article and Gitea's release blog into vulnerability-management datamodels. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because VM inventory is not expressible on their event-shaped log sources. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated dev/test Gitea instances not reachable from the internet (still worth patching but lower priority)
  • TVM keying on container image digest may mis-map or miss containerized Gitea deployments
  • Forgejo forks mis-attributed as Gitea by the scanner
  • Instances already reconfigured with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 but not yet version-upgraded (mitigated, still flagged)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each flagged host confirm the exact Gitea build and whether reverse-proxy auth (ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION) is enabled and internet-exposed. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.3+ (or 1.26.4); as an interim mitigation set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 and disable reverse-proxy auth if not required. Step 3 (hunt): For any host that was exposed, retro-hunt web/proxy logs for X-WEBAUTH-USER (UC1) and contact from 159.26.98.241 (UC2) to determine if it was probed or compromised before patching.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20896")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20896")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-20896")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-20896")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Adobe ColdFusion server process spawning OS command interpreter (CVE-2026-48282 RCE landing)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Webshell (.cfm/.cfc/.jsp) written into ColdFusion webroot/CFIDE by CF process (CVE-2026-48282 file write)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Adobe ColdFusion server process spawning OS command interpreter (CVE-2026-48282 RCE landing) AIExploitation High
Hunts the ColdFusion JVM/service (coldfusion.exe, or java.exe under a cfusion install path) spawning cmd/powershell/whoami/net/certutil etc. This is the post-RCE command-execution signal for CVE-2026-48282 exploitation, where an unauthenticated directory-traversal file-write is followed by shell commands running under the ColdFusion service account. Rationale: Pivots on the real ColdFusion service binaries (coldfusion.exe / java.exe under a cfusion path) as parent, which per Rapid7 and BleepingComputer is the exact process that spawns shells after ColdFusion RCE; parent+child pairing keeps FP low. External sources confirm CVE-2026-48282 is an arbitrary-file-write/traversal RCE. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/07/17/etr-active-exploitation-of-multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-coldfusion-flaws-exploited-in-attacks-to-drop-webshells/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ColdFusion scheduled tasks or CFML apps legitimately invoking cfexecute to run cmd/net for admin automation
  • Deployment/monitoring scripts run by the CF service account (e.g., health checks calling whoami/net)
  • ColdFusion updater/installer spawning cmd during patch application
  • Backup or AV agents that shell out under the java.exe of an unrelated app sharing a 'cfusion'-like path
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\ColdFusion2023\\cfusion\\lib\\updates","hf-updater") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "scheduletask")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and command line of the shell child; check whether the ColdFusion host is internet-facing and still on 2025.9/2023.20 or earlier (unpatched to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21). Correlate the spawn time against IIS/W3C request logs for a preceding traversal/write request. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process, and pull the ColdFusion service offline or block inbound 80/443 at the WAF; rotate the CF service account and datasource credentials. 3) Hunt: search for freshly written .cfm/.cfc/.jsp files under CFIDE/wwwroot (UC2), outbound C2 from the CF process, new local accounts, and reuse of the same source IP across other CF instances.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe"))
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("coldfusion","cfusion"))
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has "coldfusion.exe" or ParentProcessName has "jrunsvc.exe" or ParentProcessName has "cfexec.exe")
     or (ParentProcessName has "java.exe" and (ParentProcessName has "coldfusion" or ParentProcessName has "cfusion"))
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ColdFusion Server Process Spawning OS Command Interpreter
id: 7c3f2b1a-9d4e-4a2c-8b6f-1e5a0c2d7f91
description: Detects the Adobe ColdFusion service (coldfusion.exe or java.exe under a cfusion install path) spawning shell/LOLBin children, indicating CVE-2026-48282 post-exploitation command execution.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-adobe-coldfusion-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/
  - https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/07/17/etr-active-exploitation-of-multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_cf:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\coldfusion.exe'
      - '\jrunsvc.exe'
      - '\cfexec.exe'
  parent_java:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\java.exe'
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'coldfusion'
      - 'cfusion'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\nltest.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
  condition: (parent_cf or parent_java) and child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\coldfusion.exe OR *\\ColdFusion.exe OR *\\jrunsvc.exe OR *\\cfexec.exe) OR (@ParentImage:(*\\java.exe OR *\\Java.exe) AND @ParentImage:(*coldfusion* OR *cfusion*))) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\wscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ParentBaseFileName=/^(coldfusion|jrunsvc|cfexec)\.exe$/i OR (ParentBaseFileName=/^java\.exe$/i AND ParentImageFileName=/(coldfusion|cfusion)/i))
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|net1?|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|wget|nltest|cscript|wscript)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe","java.exe")) AND (Processes.parent_process_name!="java.exe" OR Processes.parent_process="*coldfusion*" OR Processes.parent_process="*cfusion*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nltest.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe","java.exe")) AND (Processes.parent_process_name!="java.exe" OR Processes.parent_process="*coldfusion*" OR Processes.parent_process="*cfusion*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nltest.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Webshell (.cfm/.cfc/.jsp) written into ColdFusion webroot/CFIDE by CF process (CVE-2026-48282 file write) AIInstallation High
Hunts new or modified .cfm/.cfc/.cfml/.jsp files landing under ColdFusion web roots (CFIDE, wwwroot, cf_scripts) written by the ColdFusion service process. CVE-2026-48282 is a directory-traversal arbitrary-file-write, so a CF-authored script file appearing in the webroot at runtime is the webshell-drop primitive itself. Rationale: Uses the concrete webshell landing sites named by Rapid7/BleepingComputer for ColdFusion (CFIDE, wwwroot, cf_scripts) plus CF-native script extensions, gated to writes performed by the ColdFusion process — the exact arbitrary-file-write behaviour of CVE-2026-48282 rather than a generic file-drop rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-coldfusion-flaws-exploited-in-attacks-to-drop-webshells/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/03/21/etr-rapid7-observed-exploitation-of-adobe-coldfusion/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Applying ColdFusion 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21 (the patch itself rewrites .cfm/.cfc files under cfusion)
  • Legitimate CFML application deployments / CI publishing new templates into wwwroot
  • Developers hot-editing .cfm pages on a staging CF server
  • ColdFusion Administrator regenerating cf_scripts/ajax assets after a config change
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hf-updater","\\updates\\","install.jar") or FolderPath has "\\cfusion\\lib\\updates\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped file — webshells contain <cfexecute>, cfhttp, eval, or base64 blobs and are short/obfuscated vs legitimate templates; note the write timestamp and the CF process command line. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, snapshot it for forensics, isolate the host, and take the CF instance offline until patched to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21. 3) Hunt: pivot on the file hash across all CF hosts, review IIS logs for GET/POST to that path (attacker interacting with the shell), and correlate with UC1 shell-spawn events and outbound C2.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".cfm" or FileName endswith ".cfc" or FileName endswith ".cfml" or FileName endswith ".jsp"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\CFIDE\", @"\wwwroot\", @"\cfusion\", @"\cf_scripts\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe","java.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName has_any (".cfm",".cfc",".cfml",".jsp")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\CFIDE\", @"\wwwroot\", @"\cfusion\", @"\cf_scripts\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("coldfusion.exe","java.exe","jrunsvc.exe","cfexec.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Webshell File Written to ColdFusion Webroot by CF Process
id: b2e91f4d-6a37-4c58-9f21-3d0c7a5e8b42
description: Detects .cfm/.cfc/.cfml/.jsp files created or modified under ColdFusion web roots (CFIDE, wwwroot, cf_scripts) by the ColdFusion service process, the arbitrary-file-write webshell drop of CVE-2026-48282.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-coldfusion-flaws-exploited-in-attacks-to-drop-webshells/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-adobe-coldfusion-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/06
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\coldfusion.exe'
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\jrunsvc.exe'
      - '\cfexec.exe'
  ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.cfm'
      - '.cfc'
      - '.cfml'
      - '.jsp'
  path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\CFIDE\'
      - '\wwwroot\'
      - '\cfusion\'
      - '\cf_scripts\'
  condition: proc and ext and path
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.cfm OR *.CFM OR *.cfc OR *.cfml OR *.jsp OR *.JSP) @TargetFilename:(*\\CFIDE\\* OR *\\cfide\\* OR *\\wwwroot\\* OR *\\cfusion\\* OR *\\cf_scripts\\*) @Image:(*\\coldfusion.exe OR *\\ColdFusion.exe OR *\\java.exe OR *\\Java.exe OR *\\jrunsvc.exe OR *\\cfexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.(cfm|cfc|cfml|jsp)$/i
| regex("\\\\(CFIDE|wwwroot|cfusion|cf_scripts)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(coldfusion|java|jrunsvc|cfexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.cfm" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfc" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfml") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\CFIDE\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\cfusion\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\cf_scripts\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.cfm" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfc" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfml") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\CFIDE\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wwwroot\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\cfusion\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\cf_scripts\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Directory-traversal / arbitrary-write request to ColdFusion endpoints in web logs (CVE-2026-48282 exploit attempt) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to ColdFusion paths (CFIDE, cf_scripts, .cfm/.cfc handlers) carrying directory-traversal sequences in the URI or query string. CVE-2026-48282 is exploited unauthenticated via path traversal leading to arbitrary file write, so traversal-laden requests to a CF server are the initial-access attempt on the wire. Rationale: Targets the exploit primitive KEVIntel/Watchtowr describe for CVE-2026-48282 (unauthenticated directory traversal → arbitrary file write) on the one telemetry that actually sees the inbound request: web-server/WAF logs scoped to ColdFusion URIs with traversal tokens. Left defender_kql empty because Defender AH carries no IIS request logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-adobe-coldfusion-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/multiple-adobe-coldfusion-vulnerabilities/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/adobe-patches-7-cvss-100-flaws-in.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing CF paths with traversal payloads
  • Security researchers / bug-bounty testing against the CF admin console
  • Legitimate CF apps that pass '..'-containing values in query strings (relative path params)
  • WAF already blocking the request (scStatus 403) — noise if not filtered to successful writes
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200,201,206,301,302) and cIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check scStatus — a 200/201/302 on a traversal request to a .cfm/CFIDE path is high concern; capture cIP and user-agent and geolocate (early exploitation was seen from an India-geolocated IP). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, and if the request succeeded treat the host as compromised — take CF offline and patch to 2025 Update 10 / 2023 Update 21. 3) Hunt: correlate the request time with UC2 file-write and UC1 shell-spawn on the same host, and sweep other internet-facing CF instances (Shadowserver counts ~800 exposed) for the same source IP or user-agent.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/CFIDE/","/cf_scripts/","/cfusion/",".cfm",".cfc")
| where csUriStem has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%255c","..%c0%af") or csUriQuery has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%255c")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="*/CFIDE/*" OR Web.uri_path="*/cf_scripts/*" OR Web.uri_path="*.cfm*" OR Web.uri_path="*.cfc*") AND (Web.uri_path="*..*" OR Web.uri_query="*..*" OR Web.uri_path="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.uri_query="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.uri_path="*..%255c*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.uri_path Web.uri_query Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="*/CFIDE/*" OR Web.uri_path="*/cf_scripts/*" OR Web.uri_path="*.cfm*" OR Web.uri_path="*.cfc*") AND (Web.uri_path="*..*" OR Web.uri_query="*..*" OR Web.uri_path="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.uri_query="*%2e%2e*" OR Web.uri_path="*..%255c*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.uri_path Web.uri_query Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48282")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48282")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48282")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48282")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 18 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A suspected China-nexus threat activity cluster has been observed targeting Indian taxpayers, tax professionals, and corporate finance teams to deliver a remote access trojan designed to steal sensitive data from compromised hosts. The multi-stage campaign, codenamed Operation DragonReturn by Seqrite Labs, involves sending spear-phishing emails impersonating the Income Tax Department of India.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake 'Common Offline Utility ITR' tax tool download from govtop[.]one (Operation DragonReturn delivery) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Suspected China-Nexus Hackers Use Fake Indian Tax Filing Utility to Deploy DcRAT
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-loaded from Windows Media Player folder (DcRAT stage-2) · [LLM] DcRAT steganographic payload staged as C:\Windows\background.jpg (lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250) · [LLM] MixedSvc auto-start service persistence via 'Mixed Reality.exe' (DcRAT) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DcRAT C2 beacon to 223.26.63[.]40:2671 / exfil to kkxqbh[.]top · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Fake 'Common Offline Utility ITR' tax tool download from govtop[.]one (Operation DragonReturn delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts the initial delivery stage of Operation DragonReturn: a ZIP/EXE masquerading as India's Income Tax offline filing utility (Common_Offline_Utility_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.zip / COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.exe) dropped from the govtop[.]one/incometax lure page. Article-specific because it keys on the exact cloned government utility filename and the delivery domain, not generic ZIP downloads. Rationale: Keys on the exact cloned government utility filename (Common_Offline_Utility_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27 / COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27.exe) and delivery domain govtop[.]one/incometax named in the article and Seqrite blog — both are unique to this campaign, giving near-zero false positives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef987-564e-79dc-a057-8add6dd51d8e
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate taxpayer downloading the real Income Tax Department offline utility (real filename differs; the exact 'COU_ITR-1_to_4' abbreviation + .exe is the malicious variant)
  • Security researcher/analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Backup/archival tools copying an already-quarantined sample
  • EDR test files named to mimic the campaign during purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one" or FileName has "COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess (browser/mail client) and FileOriginUrl for the drop; confirm the ZIP/EXE came from govtop[.]one and hash against the Seqrite IOC list. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the ZIP/EXE and any extracted COU_ITR-*.exe, block govtop[.]one at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check the same host for a subsequent nvdaHelperRemote.dll write to C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\, a background.jpg drop in C:\Windows, and creation of the MixedSvc service.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName has_any ("Common_Offline_Utility_ITR", "COU_ITR-1_to_4_AY2026-27")
   or (FileName endswith ".zip" and FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one")
   or FileOriginUrl has "govtop.one/incometax"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "govtop.one"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-loaded from Windows Media Player folder (DcRAT stage-2) AIInstallation High
Detects the DcRAT DLL side-loading step where a 504 KB malicious nvdaHelperRemote.dll is planted in and loaded from C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\ — a masquerade of the legitimate NVDA screen-reader component. Article-specific: the legit DLL never lives under Windows Media Player, so path+name is the anomaly. Rationale: nvdaHelperRemote.dll is a legitimate NVDA screen-reader file; its presence/loading under C:\Program Files\Windows Media Player\ (per the article and Seqrite process diagram) is a hard masquerade indicator unique to this DcRAT chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine NVDA install writing nvdaHelperRemote.dll — but to \Program Files\NVDA\, never Windows Media Player
  • Admin manually copying accessibility DLLs into the wrong directory (rare)
  • Software packaging tool relocating DLLs during a repackage
  • EDR/AV quarantine-restore replacing the file in its captured path
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\NVDA\" or FolderPath has @"\NVDA\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the loading process (COU_ITR-*.exe or Mixed Reality.exe) and hash of the DLL; a ~504 KB unsigned DLL under Windows Media Player is confirmation. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL and its loader, kill the loading process. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for C:\Windows\background.jpg, the MixedSvc service, and outbound to 223.26.63[.]40:2671.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nvdaHelperRemote.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows Media Player\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "nvdaHelperRemote.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has "Windows Media Player"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DcRAT steganographic payload staged as C:\Windows\background.jpg (lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250) AIInstallation High
Detects the image-based payload concealment step: the loader fetches lllyd.jpg from 204.194.48[.]250 and writes it as C:\Windows\background.jpg, from which a second-stage DLL is carved. Article-specific: a .jpg written to the Windows root by a non-system process paired with the hardcoded staging server. Rationale: C:\Windows\background.jpg written by a user-space process, plus the hardcoded staging IP 204.194.48[.]250/lllyd.jpg, are both explicit in the article and Seqrite diagram; a JPG in the Windows root is inherently anomalous and survives C2 IP rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OEM/desktop-personalization software staging a wallpaper named background.jpg (usually under \Windows\Web\Wallpaper, not the Windows root)
  • Sysadmin GPO deploying a corporate wallpaper to C:\Windows (verify the writing process is TrustedInstaller/GPO, not a user EXE)
  • Third-party theme installer dropping images
  • Imaging/MDT task-sequence writing default wallpaper during provisioning
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "svchost.exe", "msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process — if a recently-downloaded EXE (COU_ITR-*.exe / Mixed Reality.exe) wrote it, treat as confirmed; check for a preceding fetch from 204.194.48[.]250. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine background.jpg and the writing binary, block 204.194.48[.]250. 3) Hunt: look for the extracted 504 KB nvdaHelperRemote.dll under Windows Media Player and the MixedSvc service on the same and peer hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "background.jpg"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows\background.jpg"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "background.jpg"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\background.jpg"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MixedSvc auto-start service persistence via 'Mixed Reality.exe' (DcRAT) AIInstallation High
Detects the persistence step where the malware copies itself to 'Mixed Reality.exe' and registers an auto-start Windows service named MixedSvc to survive reboot. Article-specific: both the service name (MixedSvc) and the masqueraded binary name are unique to Operation DragonReturn. Rationale: Service name MixedSvc and self-copied binary 'Mixed Reality.exe' are explicitly named in the article, Seqrite blog and process diagram — a distinctive persistence signature that no legitimate software uses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Mixed Reality / WMR platform components (legit binaries are MixedRealityPortal.exe / signed by Microsoft under System32 or WindowsApps — not a bare 'Mixed Reality.exe' from a user path)
  • Developer/test service named similarly during MR app development
  • Backup agent re-registering services after restore
  • Sysadmin installing a HMD vendor driver package
Suppression filter
| where ServiceFileName !has @"\WindowsApps\" and ServiceFileName !has @"\System32\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ServiceFileName/ImagePath — a 'Mixed Reality.exe' outside System32/WindowsApps, unsigned or signed anomalously, confirms it; note the InitiatingProcess. 2) Contain: stop and delete the MixedSvc service (sc delete MixedSvc), quarantine Mixed Reality.exe, isolate host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the MixedSvc service name and for injected svchost.exe beaconing to 223.26.63[.]40:2671.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| extend SvcName = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).ServiceName), ImagePath = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).ImagePath)
| where SvcName =~ "MixedSvc" or ImagePath has "Mixed Reality.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SvcName, ImagePath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "MixedSvc" or ServiceFileName has "Mixed Reality.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DcRAT C2 beacon to 223.26.63[.]40:2671 / exfil to kkxqbh[.]top AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the DcRAT command-and-control and data-exfiltration stage: encrypted beacon to the hardcoded C2 223.26.63[.]40 on non-standard port 2671, and exfil to kkxqbh[.]top (plus related actor domains). Article/diagram-specific IP+port combination and exfil domain. Rationale: 223.26.63[.]40:2671 (the exact DcRAT C2 IP and port from the Seqrite diagram) and exfil domain kkxqbh[.]top are hard, campaign-unique IOCs; the non-standard port on the fixed IP makes this a low-FP alerting detection even against encrypted traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-cyber-espionage-campaign-targeting-govt-of-india-mof-tax-infrastructure-via-multi-stage-dcrat-deployment/ • https://gurucul.com/latest-threats/operation-dragonreturn-china-nexus-campaign-targeting-indias-tax-infrastructure-via-dcrat/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef987-564e-79dc-a057-8add6dd51d8e
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/scanning platforms (Shodan, Censys) probing 223.26.63[.]40 from a sanctioned scanner host
  • Analyst sandbox detonation generating the beacon deliberately
  • Stale IOC reuse if the ChinaNet IP is later reassigned to benign hosting (validate recency)
  • Security proxy/sinkhole re-resolving the exfil domains during enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process — if it is svchost.exe launched from an unusual path or injected by MixedSvc/Mixed Reality.exe, treat as confirmed DcRAT. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 223.26.63[.]40 and kkxqbh[.]top (+related domains) at firewall/DNS, kill the process and MixedSvc service. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts contacting the C2 IP/domains, then back-trace to the govtop[.]one download, nvdaHelperRemote.dll side-load and background.jpg drop to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "223.26.63.40" and RemotePort == 2671)
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "223.26.63.40" and DstPortNumber == 2671)
   or DstHostname in~ ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
   or Url has_any ("kkxqbh.top", "ikkkkddd.com", "1kkkkddd.com", "simaqz.com", "jiayingjing.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
